newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay stocks close higher, pivotals lead uptrend.
newsitem.headline: Bombay stocks close higher, pivotals lead uptrend.

text.p: Bombay shares ended higher on Thursday as investors awaited the outcome of a key United Front meeting to elect a new leader, traders said.
The alliance is due to meet on Friday at 10 a.m. (0430 GMT) to discuss replacing caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda as its leader, Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan said.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index jumped 47.70 points, or 1.31 percent, to close at a provisional 3695.14.
Traders said top banking stock State Bank of India and petrochemicals giant Reliance Industries led the uptrend.
"The general mood is optimistic," said a chief dealer at a local brokerage. "People are hopeful of the budget going through."
Shares of India's largest private firm Reliance surged 12.0 rupees, or 4.5 percent, to close near the day's high of 280.
Traders said speculators were bidders ahead of the company's results for the financial year ended March 31, 1997 which are due on April 22.
They said speculators were also taking positions in the stock ahead of its entering a no-delivery period on the Bombay and National bourses next week.
A no-delivery period allows speculators to trade in the stock without taking delivery for around one month.
Traders said bank stocks were in the limelight as investors bought in response to the central bank's market-friendly credit policy.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) loosened its credit policy for the first six months of 1997/98 (April-March) to bring down interest rates and keep economic growth on track while containing inflation.
"The stock market is looking good in the immediate term," said the head of trading at a foreign brokerage.
"The credit policy has increased the liquidity in the system and before this is really utilised by business, there will be a lot of excess liquidity in the market," he said.
RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said a number of steps had been taken in the credit policy to improve the credit delivery system.
"We have given greater autonomy to banks to determine working capital limits for borrowers and also eased norms on consortium lending," he said.
Shares of largest commercial bank State Bank of India climbed 9.50 rupees, or 3.3 percent, to close at 296 in large volumes.
Oriental Bank of Commerce shares rose 3.0 rupees, or 4.1 percent, to 75.50 and HDFC Bank gained 3.75 rupees, or 7.2 percent, to 55.75.

"The policy doesn't add directly to banks' bottomlines but the fact that they have been given much more operational freedom is a big plus point, especially for the frontline banks," said a banking analyst at a foreign brokerage.
"It was an excellent policy and is bound to make liquidity easier," said a fund manager.
"If only the politics would sort itself out you could really see the market running. We need to get the political issue out of the way," he added.
